To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the public and Congress have similar levels of polarization on the issues that they know about.
the public is not well informed about the political alignment of many issues.

1) the distribution of issue positions of the public is far less polarized than that of the Senate; 2) the subset of the public who demonstrate knowledge of political issues is far more polarized; 3) this subset of the public is more likely to hold issue positions that are consistent with their partisan identities; and 4) this subset of public opinion is more polarized than that held by the Senate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the U.S. Congress represents the public's preferences.
a question that has received little empirical attention: Does the U.S. Congress accurately represent the public’s preferences on issues?
the question of how the distribution of issue positions in the public compares to the positions taken by Congress, and how that distribution might change if the public were to become better informed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Congress represents the public's opinion as it is, and as it might be if the public was better informed.
Congress is representative of the public opinion that would exist were citizens better informed.
Congress is representative, but only in a limited way.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Congress is not representative in the sense that its members hold issue positions that are identical to those of the public.
the public is more polarized than previously thought, but not by as much as Congress.
the Senate represents the public as it might be rather than as it is.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is not enough to know the public opinion distribution on a single issue to assess representation.
the quality of Congressional representativeness is higher than previous work has shown, and that the public is more polarized than previous work has suggested.
Congress is not as unrepresentative of the public as it is commonly thought to be.
